title: UPOV TGP/14/6: Glossary of Terms Used in UPOV Documents
claims_verified: Campanulate has an inflated tube widening distally; filiform is thread-like; hastate has triangular basal lobes directed outwards and is distinguished from sagittate; pubescent/pubescence is synonymous with hairy/hairiness in plant-character terminology; reflexed means an angle over 180 degrees or an abrupt abaxial/downward bend and is distinguished from recurved; spreading is directed outward; ascending is routed to gradually upward orientation; entire is an undivided, untoothed, unlobed margin; sessile means stalkless and directly attached; viscid means sticky or gummy; lanate and sericeous specify distinct trichome arrangements.

title: Missouri Botanical Garden Botanical Latin: campanulatus
claims_verified: Campanulate denotes a bell-like form with a broadened rim and is distinguished from neighboring tubular forms.

title: Missouri Botanical Garden Botanical Latin: filiform
claims_verified: Filiform denotes a thread-like, slender, elongate form; the cited Fernald gloss additionally specifies long, slender, and terete.

title: Missouri Botanical Garden Botanical Latin: hastatus
claims_verified: Hastate has approximately triangular basal lobes directed outward at wide angles.

title: PlantNET New South Wales Flora glossary: hastate
claims_verified: A hastate leaf has a narrow pointed lamina with basal lobes spreading roughly at right angles to the petiole.

title: Color: Universal Language and Dictionary of Names
claims_verified: The dictionary maps crimson and scarlet to multiple ISCC-NBS blocks depending on the source; neither word has one source-independent block.

title: The ISCC-NBS Method of Designating Colors and a Dictionary of Color Names
claims_verified: Published central prototypes include vivid red and vivid reddish orange blocks, but those block prototypes do not by themselves define the full botanical uses of crimson or scarlet.

title: American Orchid Society Orchid Glossary
claims_verified: An orchid labellum is the modified petal called the lip; a pseudobulb is a thickened stem portion rather than a true bulb; alate means winged, having wings or wing-like parts.

title: American Orchid Society Orchid Glossary: downy
claims_verified: Downy means covered with very short, weak, soft hairs.

title: MADS-Box Genes and Their Role in Orchid Development
claims_verified: The orchid perianth has an inner whorl of three petals, one of which is the specialized lip or labellum.

title: NYBG Steere Herbarium glossary: corolla tube
claims_verified: A corolla tube is the lower fused portion of a gamopetalous corolla.

title: NYBG Steere Herbarium glossary: corolla throat
claims_verified: The glossary defines the corolla throat as the opening into the corolla tube, which conflicts with sources using throat for a surrounding distal tube region.

title: Bilabiate Flowers: The Ultimate Response to Bees?
claims_verified: Upper and lower lips are functional/morphological components of bilabiate constructions; the unqualified word lip is not restricted to one homologous organ type.

title: NYBG Steere Herbarium glossary: pseudobulb
claims_verified: A pseudobulb is a specially modified, swollen stem used to store food and water.

title: NYBG Steere Herbarium glossary: tunic
claims_verified: A tunic is an outer dry papery covering of a bulb or corm.

title: NYBG Steere Herbarium glossary: corona
claims_verified: Corona denotes a floral structure between petals and stamens that may be derived from either organ system.

title: Corona development and floral nectaries of Asclepiadeae
claims_verified: Asclepiadeae coronas can be androecial or corolline; apparent attachment to the corolla does not alone establish developmental origin.

title: A roadmap of haustorium morphogenesis in parasitic plants
claims_verified: A parasitic-plant haustorium penetrates host tissues and establishes transfer; terminal haustoria are root-derived, while lateral haustoria may arise from root or stem tissues.

title: Towards a Standardization of Terminology of the Climbing Habit in Plants
claims_verified: A climber becomes unable to mechanically sustain its stem without external support; liana and vine distinguish woody and non-woody climbers; scrambling and twining are distinct climbing mechanisms.

title: NYBG Steere Herbarium glossary: apex
claims_verified: Apex denotes the tip or distal end of a structure such as a stem or leaf; PO separately distinguishes an extended apex region from its apical-most tip in several existing classes.

title: NYBG Steere Herbarium glossary: base
claims_verified: Base denotes the bottom or proximal end of a structure such as a stem, leaf blade, or flower.

title: NYBG Steere Herbarium glossary: lobe
claims_verified: A lobe is a rounded projection from the margin or base of a two-dimensional structure such as a leaf or bract.

title: NYBG Steere Herbarium glossary: leaf margin lobed
claims_verified: A lobed leaf margin bears rounded blade projections cut less than halfway to the midrib in this glossary; this boundary differs from PO's current one-quarter-or-more sinus threshold for a phyllome lamina lobe.

title: NYBG Steere Herbarium glossary: leaf margin entire
claims_verified: An entire leaf margin is smooth and lacks serrations or crenations.

title: NYBG Steere Herbarium glossary: cyathium
claims_verified: A cyathium is an inflorescence of several naked staminate flowers, usually one naked pistillate flower, and a subtending cup-shaped involucre, characteristic of Euphorbia.

title: NYBG Steere Herbarium glossary: hair
claims_verified: The botanical hair entry redirects to trichome and says trichome is the more correct term for plants.

title: NYBG Steere Herbarium glossary: trichome
claims_verified: A trichome is a hair-like epidermal outgrowth, and trichome is preferred over hair in botany.

title: American Orchid Society Orchid Glossary: hairs and trichome
claims_verified: Hairs is a general name for many small slender plant outgrowths; trichome is the correct botanical term for a hair-like epidermal outgrowth such as a hair or bristle.

title: NYBG Steere Herbarium glossary: trunk as first-order unbranched portion
claims_verified: In trees, trunk is defined as the unbranched first-order portion and equated with bole; the downloaded page appears to contain a typographical error in the bearer word.

title: NYBG Steere Herbarium glossary: trunk as main stem
claims_verified: A trunk is the main stem of a tree; the source additionally includes buttresses and prop roots, which must not be carried into a strict stem subclass because those structures need not be stem tissue.

title: NYBG Steere Herbarium glossary: frond
claims_verified: This glossary restricts frond to a fern leaf and the conspicuous sporophyte structure; that restriction does not cover the dominant Saudi palm-frond usage.

title: Florida Invasive Plants glossary: frond
claims_verified: The glossary, whose definitions are taken from Guide to the Vascular Plants of Florida, defines a frond as the leaf of a fern or palm.

title: Flora of Australia Glossary — Ferns, Cycads, Conifers and Vascular plants
claims_verified: A frond is a leaf, especially of a fern, cycad, or palm, including its lamina and stipe or petiole.

title: NYBG Steere Herbarium glossary: pinna
claims_verified: A pinna is the primary division of a compound leaf, especially a fern leaf.

title: NYBG Steere Herbarium glossary: pinnule
claims_verified: A pinnule is a secondary or higher-order division of a fern compound leaf; the downloaded page contains a repeated phrase in its worked example, so only the clear first clause is used.

title: NYBG Steere Herbarium glossary: annual
claims_verified: An annual plant completes the interval from seed to maturity and death in one year or less; the page explicitly contrasts annual, biennial, and perennial.

title: NYBG Steere Herbarium glossary: perennial
claims_verified: A perennial is a plant that lives and produces seeds for three or more years; the page explicitly contrasts annual and biennial.

title: NYBG Steere Herbarium glossary: trifoliolate
claims_verified: Trifoliolate means having three leaflets.

title: NYBG Steere Herbarium glossary: winged
claims_verified: Winged or alate means having a thin conspicuous ridge running along a structure such as a stem, leaf rachis, ovary, or fruit.

title: NYBG Steere Herbarium glossary: reflexed
claims_verified: Reflexed means abruptly bent backward or downward.

title: NYBG Steere Herbarium glossary: solitary flower
claims_verified: A solitary-flower construction specifies one flower in the inflorescence context; this conflicts with PO's current inflorescence minimum of two flowers and is therefore treated as a cardinality phenotype, not a new inflorescence entity.

title: NYBG Steere Herbarium glossary: caespitose (cespitose)
claims_verified: Caespitose or cespitose means growing in dense clumps or tufts; the clumps are also called tussocks.

title: NYBG Steere Herbarium glossary: viscid
claims_verified: Viscid means sticky; UPOV further distinguishes viscid from resinous, where resin causes the stickiness.

title: NYBG Steere Herbarium glossary: lanate
claims_verified: Lanate means woolly, usually as a type of pubescence; UPOV specifies long, somewhat matted, tangled trichomes and distinguishes shorter denser tomentose hairs.

title: NYBG Steere Herbarium glossary: sericeous
claims_verified: Sericeous means silky, with long soft slender somewhat appressed hairs; UPOV likewise specifies fine, long, appressed trichomes.

title: Flora of Australia Glossary — Ferns, Cycads, Conifers and Vascular plants
claims_verified: The official glossary operationally distinguishes aquatic, capitate, crown, costate or ribbed, crisped, deciduous, evergreen, farinaceous, keeled, persistent, petaloid, procumbent, runner, stolon, unisexual, whorl, and the different botanical senses of wing.

title: PlantNET New South Wales Flora glossary: C
claims_verified: Capitate means head-shaped or arranged in a head-like cluster; clasping means surrounding or embracing an axis, such as a lamina surrounding a stem.

title: PlantNET New South Wales Flora glossary: D–E
claims_verified: Dissected means divided at least partially into segments; deciduous distinguishes seasonally falling organs and plants losing leaves for part of the year; evergreen plants bear leaves throughout the year.

title: PlantNET New South Wales Flora glossary: F–H
claims_verified: Farina is a fine mealy powder on a plant surface; frond denotes a fern or cycad leaf and is sometimes used for a large compound palm leaf; floccose means covered with soft woolly hairs that are entangled and tend to rub off.

title: PlantNET New South Wales Flora glossary: I–L
claims_verified: Latex is fluid exuded from cut plant surfaces and is not necessarily milky; lax means loose or not compact; lineolate means marked with fine or obscure lines.

title: PlantNET New South Wales Flora glossary: M–O
claims_verified: Mealy means covered with coarse flour-like powder.

title: PlantNET New South Wales Flora glossary: P
claims_verified: The glossary separates palmate leaf and venation senses, defines persistent relative to maturation of the bearer, petaloid by petal-like colour and texture, plicate as longitudinally folded, and procumbent as trailing or spreading over the ground.

title: PlantNET New South Wales Flora glossary: S
claims_verified: The glossary defines sheath as a tubular or rolled organ part, shrub by its woody much-branched growth form, stinging hair by a hollow hair seated on a secreting gland, and stolon as a horizontal above-ground stem rooting at nodes.

title: PlantNET New South Wales Flora glossary: T–U
claims_verified: Unisexual means bearing only male or only female reproductive organs; united means fused together; trifoliolate means a leaf with three leaflets.

title: PlantNET New South Wales Flora glossary: V–Z
claims_verified: Whorl is a ring of leaves, bracts, or floral parts at one axis level; wing has distinct fruit or seed flange, stem or petiole flange, and Fabaceae petal senses; woolly denotes dense matted long hairs.

title: NYBG Steere Herbarium glossary: clasping
claims_verified: Clasping or amplexicaul means at least partially enclosing an axis, such as a leaf base partially surrounding its stem.

title: Royal Horticultural Society gardening glossary: foliage
claims_verified: The RHS glossary defines foliage as leaves and independently distinguishes annual, perennial, deciduous, and evergreen plant life-history terms.

title: Chromotaxia seu Nomenclator colorum polyglottus ad usum botanicorum et zoologorum
claims_verified: Saccardo provides a botanical and zoological colour vocabulary with physical plates and recognition exemplars, including silver as white with metallic lustre, chestnut pericarp, roasted cacao for chocolate-brown, salmon flesh, Rosa centifolia petals for rosy, citrus epicarp for lemon-yellow, freshly dried wheat or rice culms for straw-coloured, and cow-milk cream for cream-coloured.

title: Color Standards and Color Nomenclature
claims_verified: Ridgway supplies physical colour standards and explicitly warns that unstandardized names such as lemon, chestnut, lilac, and olive vary; source-qualified chips exist for lemon yellow, chestnut, chocolate, mahogany red, olive, rose pink, salmon color, and straw yellow.

title: Royal Horticultural Society herbarium: pressing and collecting samples
claims_verified: The RHS herbarium protocol instructs collectors to record colours that may change on drying by reference to the RHS Colour Chart while the material is fresh.

title: Royal Horticultural Society herbarium: nomenclatural standards
claims_verified: RHS nomenclatural-standard guidance treats RHS Colour Chart references as part of a diagnostic cultivar description.

title: UPOV TWO/49/20: Definition of Color Groups from RHS Colour Charts
claims_verified: The sixth-edition RHS chart has 920 patches and 190 objective colour names determined using CIE coordinates and Munsell; the document also records naming inconsistencies and distinguishes precise chip references from coarser colour groups.

title: Gene Ontology go-basic release 2026-06-15
claims_verified: The pinned FLOPO GO import module extracts GO:0008150 biological_process from the official 2026-06-15 go-basic release; future process terms must be extracted with their ancestry from the same pinned release.

title: Multiple facets of laticifer cells
claims_verified: The review describes latex as laticifer cytoplasmic fluid, commonly a suspension or emulsion of particles in an aqueous phase, held in living laticifer cells and capable of exuding when laticiferous tissue is damaged.
